# dsh-plugin-dbgraph
**Database structure the agent already knows, so it answers with one tool call instead of five.**

A DeepSeek Harness plugin that indexes a remote
database's *catalog* — every table, column, comment,

key, index, and a bounded sample of enum
literals — into a local SQLite index under `~/.dsh/dbgraph

`. The model reads that index (and a digest
of it placed directly in the system prompt) instead of s

pending round-trips on `SHOW TABLES` and
`DESCRIBE`, then fetches the actual values with exactly one

trips on `SHOW TABLES` and
`DESCRIBE`, then fetches the actual values with exactly one network call.
## The problem it removes
Without an index, answering *"what is 张三's password?"* looks like this:

Four model round-trips, four network round-trips, two wrong guesses. **The expensive part is not the
database — it is the model's turns.** Each one costs seconds; a 100 ms query does not.
With dbgraph:

## Structure local, data online
| | Where | Why |
| Tables, columns, comments, keys, indexes, enum samples, row estimates | **Local index** | Zero net

work, usable offline, no credential needed to ask what a column means |
| Actual row values | **Alwa
ys the server** | A cached password is not a fast password, it is a wrong one |
Nothing derived from business data is persisted. The one data-shaped field is `enum_values_json`, a
`SELECT DISTINCT … LIMIT n` sample that teaches the model whether `status` holds `'paid'` or `1`.
## Layout
[代码示例省略，未执行]
### Why the write path is Rust
`node:sqlite` is a synchronous API. Writing ten thousand columns through it blocks the event loop fo

r
as long as the write takes — this is the same wall `dsh-plugin-codegraph` and
`dsh-plugin-sessiong

raph` hit, and both moved their kernels behind napi `AsyncTask` to get past it.
`crates/dbgraph-inde

xer` does the same: normalization, term generation, and the SQLite write run on
libuv's thread pool,
so a rebuild never stalls the host.
Measured on one machine, same catalog, same fixed clock — 500 tables / 10,000 columns:
| writer | write | index file | longest event-loop block |

| JavaScript | 1992 ms | 8.46 MiB | **1992 ms** (the whole write) |
| Rust (`AsyncTask`) | 218 ms |

**9.1× faster, and the blocking cost drops 59×** — which is the number that matters, because a
two-s
econd stall is two seconds of the host doing nothing else.

The two writers are checked against each other rather than trusted: given the same catalog and the
s

ame fixed `now`, `objects`, `columns`, `edges`, `terms`, and `search` (rowids included) must match
r

ow for row, and only `meta.writer` may differ. Fixture expectations are generated by *running* the
J

avaScript writer, never hand-written, so a change on either side that is not mirrored fails the
buil

aScript writer, never hand-written, so a change on either side that is not mirrored fails the
build.
The JavaScript writer is therefore not an optimization fallback — it is the **parity reference** and
the **degradation path** (no Rust toolchain, no addon, a throwing call, an unparsable answer all fa

ll
back to it, once and quietly).
### Two things that had to be measured, not assumed

- **`node:sqlite` contentless FTS5 stores nothing you can read back.** Every column — `UNINDEXED`
on

es included — returns `NULL`; only `rowid` and `rank` survive. The index therefore uses a
*contentfu

l* table, where `object_id UNINDEXED` reads back verbatim. (The FTS5 column grammar is
also `column-

name [UNINDEXED]`: a type name in front is a parse error.)
- **`unicode61` treats a run of Chinese a

s one token.** Store `广告点击` verbatim and `MATCH '广告'`
finds nothing. So `text` holds a pre-tokenized

stream — camel/digit boundaries for ASCII, bigrams
for CJK — and queries go through the same tokeni

zer, joined with `OR` (a space means *phrase*, not
*any of these*).
### Picking a writer
`dbgraph_index` takes `writer: 'auto' | 'js' | 'rust'`:

- `js` — the JavaScript writer, always. Never touches the addon.
- `rust` — the native writer only;

a missing artifact or a throwing call fails the run rather than
quietly producing a slower index.
-

`auto` (default) — native when available; a missing artifact, a rejected call, or an unreadable
repo
rt logs **once per process** and falls back to JavaScript.
`DSH_DBGRAPH_RUST_ADDON` points at an artifact explicitly: a test hook for the fallback path, and an

escape hatch for a deployment that keeps the addon outside `crates/`. It defaults to
`crates/dbgrap
h-indexer/artifacts/dbgraph-indexer.<platform>-<arch>.node`.
One acknowledged difference: the JavaScript writer counts dangling edges (an edge naming a table the
snapshot does not contain) into `report.warnings`; the native writer drops them silently. The store

d
data is identical — only that one warning line differs.
## Index format

One SQLite file per connection, replaced wholesale on every run (write to a staging file named
`<ind

ex>.<pid>-<nonce>.tmp`, then rename). The nonce is per run, so two runs never share the staging
file
. That single decision removes incremental diffing, deletes, and half-updated indexes.
[代码示例省略，未执行]
`status.json` beside the indexes carries a digest the system-prompt section reads **synchronously**

—
a section is assembled on every model request, so opening SQLite there would be a per-step cost th

e
plugin refuses to pay.
## Two levels
| Level | Content | Where |

| **L1** | object and column names, declared types | inline, seconds — usable immediately |
| **L2**
| comments, foreign keys, indexes, row estimates, enum samples | background job |
An L1 failure to enrich never discards the structural snapshot: an index that answers "which columns
exist" is most of the value.
## Tools
| Tool | Timeout | What it does |

| `dbgraph` | 30 s | `connections` `schema` `objects` `columns` `find` `sql` `impact` `refs` |
| `db
graph_index` | 300 s | Builds or refreshes one connection (`l1` / `l2` / `full`); hands a large run
to a background job |
[该节后续省略]
